evidence.claim: Kroger's California notice at collection describes categories of personal and sensitive data collected, purposes and retention.

In its 'Your California Privacy Rights' section, Kroger says it has sold or shared personal information in the prior 12 months (for example identifiers) with categories of third parties including AdTech companies, social networks and data brokers, for purposes including marketing, interest-based advertising and business analytics; it says it does not knowingly sell or share information of consumers under 18. It offers Nevada residents an opt-out of sale. Other states are not established.
Kroger says it uses cookies to remember preferences, understand how you interact with its websites, conduct analytics, prevent fraud and support advertising and personalization.

Where state law provides the right, Kroger says you can opt out of sale or sharing for cross-context behavioral advertising through its Privacy Preference Center or by enabling an opt-out preference signal such as Global Privacy Control, which it treats as an opt-out request.
In its California section, Kroger says California residents may request deletion of personal information collected from them and retained, subject to exceptions.

Kroger's California section says it has sold or shared categories of personal information (such as identifiers) with categories of third parties including AdTech companies, social networks and data brokers in the prior 12 months, and describes opt-out rights and preference signals; details for other states are not established here.

Exodus Privacy static analysis of version 95.3 (report dated June 25, 2026) found code signatures for 9 known tracker SDK(s): Adobe Experience Cloud, AltBeacon, Dynatrace (analytics), Google CrashLytics (crash reporting), Google Firebase Analytics (analytics), Inmobi, OpenTelemetry (OpenCensus, OpenTracing) (analytics), Qualtrics, Salesforce Marketing Cloud. A signature shows the SDK is present, not what data it sends.
